name: Jejunum and ileum (small intestine)
func: The long, coiled middle of the gut where most nutrients are absorbed into the blood. The jejunum takes up most sugars, proteins and fats; the ileum reclaims bile acids and vitamin B12.

levels.kid:
After the duodenum, your small intestine keeps going, and going, and going! The **jejunum** and **ileum** are the long, twisty middle part, all curled up in the middle of your tummy like a garden hose. If you stretched it out, it would be longer than a car!

This is where your body takes in the good stuff from food. The inside isn't smooth: it's covered in millions of tiny finger-like bumps called **villi**, like the fluffy loops on a towel. They make the surface huge, so lots of food bits can soak into your blood.

The jejunum comes first and grabs most of the sugars, proteins and fats. The ileum comes next and grabs the last bits, plus vitamin B12 and the helpers from bile so they can be used again.
levels.hs:
The **jejunum** and **ileum** together are about **3–6 metres** long (estimates vary a lot; it measures longer after death, when muscle tone is lost). The jejunum is roughly the first **two-fifths** and the ileum the last **three-fifths**, with no sharp border between them.

They start at the **duodenojejunal flexure** (left upper abdomen, about L2) and end at the **ileocaecal junction** in the right lower quadrant, where the ileum opens into the **caecum** of the large intestine through the **ileocaecal valve**.

Unlike the duodenum, they're **intraperitoneal**, hanging on a fan-shaped fold called the **mesentery**. Its root is only about 15 cm long, running diagonally from the left upper abdomen to the right iliac fossa, crossing the duodenum, aorta, IVC and right ureter. This lets the coils move freely. They sit in the middle and lower abdomen, framed by the colon and covered in front by the **greater omentum**.

Differences you can see:
- **Jejunum**: mostly upper left; thicker wall, wider, redder; tall, crowded **circular folds**; fewer, longer **vasa recta** (straight arteries) with few arcades.
- **Ileum**: mostly lower right; thinner, paler; fewer folds; more fat in the mesentery; many short arterial **arcades**; clumps of lymphoid tissue called **Peyer's patches**.
levels.college:
The absorptive surface is amplified at three levels: **circular folds** (plicae circulares, about 3×), **villi** (about 10×) and **microvilli** forming the **brush border** (about 20×), giving a surface of roughly 30 m² by recent estimates (older textbooks cited about 200 m²; sources disagree).

The epithelium contains **enterocytes** (absorptive), **goblet cells** (mucus, increasing distally), **enteroendocrine cells**, **tuft cells**, and at the crypt base, **Paneth cells** (antimicrobial **defensins** and lysozyme) and **stem cells**. The lining renews every **3–5 days**, one of the fastest-renewing tissues in the body.

**Absorption sites**:
- **Jejunum**: most carbohydrates (as monosaccharides), amino acids and small peptides, fats, water-soluble vitamins and folate.
- **Terminal ileum**: **vitamin B12** (bound to intrinsic factor, via the **cubilin** receptor) and **bile acids** (via the apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter, **ASBT**). About 95% of bile acids are reabsorbed and returned to the liver in the **enterohepatic circulation**.

**Blood supply**: from the **superior mesenteric artery (SMA)**, via 15–18 jejunal and ileal branches forming arcades and then vasa recta, and the **ileocolic artery** for the terminal ileum. Venous blood drains to the **superior mesenteric vein** and then the **portal vein**, taking absorbed nutrients to the liver first.

**Lymph**: fat is absorbed into **lacteals** (lymph vessels in each villus) as **chylomicrons**, reaching the bloodstream via the **thoracic duct**, bypassing the liver.

**Nerves**: parasympathetic (vagus) increases motility; sympathetic (T8–T10 via the SMA plexus) reduces it. Midgut pain is felt **around the umbilicus**.

**Peyer's patches** are covered by **M cells**, which sample antigens from the lumen for the immune system.
levels.phd:
**Transporters**: glucose and galactose enter enterocytes via **SGLT1** (sodium-coupled, two Na⁺ per sugar); fructose via **GLUT5**; all three exit via **GLUT2**. The sodium gradient is maintained by the basolateral **Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase**. Because glucose transport pulls sodium, and water follows, **oral rehydration solution** (glucose plus salt) can save lives in cholera, even while the toxin drives chloride secretion through **CFTR**. Di- and tripeptides enter via the proton-coupled **PepT1**.

Fat digestion products (monoglycerides, fatty acids) form **mixed micelles** with bile acids, diffuse into enterocytes, are re-esterified in the smooth ER and packaged with **apolipoprotein B-48** into **chylomicrons**.

**Ileal brake**: nutrients reaching the ileum release **GLP-1** and **PYY** from **L cells**, slowing gastric emptying and small-bowel transit and reducing appetite. Ileal bile acid absorption also stimulates **FGF19** release, which signals the liver to reduce bile acid synthesis (by suppressing CYP7A1).

**Stem cell niche**: **LGR5+** crypt base columnar cells are the intestinal stem cells (Hans Clevers' lab, 2007), supported by Paneth cells and stromal **Wnt** and **R-spondin** signals. A single LGR5+ cell can grow into a self-organising **intestinal organoid ("mini-gut")** in a dish, now a major tool for studying disease and testing drugs on a patient's own tissue.

**Microbiome**: bacterial numbers rise from about 10³–10⁴/mL in the jejunum to 10⁷–10⁸ in the terminal ileum. The **migrating motor complex** and the ileocaecal valve keep colonic bacteria from overgrowing upstream.

**Crohn's disease** most often affects the terminal ileum; susceptibility genes include **NOD2**, ATG16L1 and IRGM, implicating bacterial sensing and **autophagy** in Paneth cells.

The **enteric nervous system** (about 400–600 million neurons, sometimes called the "second brain") runs peristalsis largely on its own.
levels.expert:
**Small bowel obstruction**: colicky central pain, vomiting (bilious, early), abdominal distension and absent passing of wind. The commonest cause in adults is **adhesions** from previous surgery, then **hernias**. Bowel sounds may be high-pitched or "tinkling". X-ray or CT shows **dilated loops** (over about 3 cm) with **air–fluid levels**; jejunal loops show the **valvulae conniventes** crossing the full width ("**stack of coins**"). **Strangulation** (constant pain, fever, raised lactate) needs urgent surgery.

**Acute mesenteric ischaemia**: an **SMA embolus** (often from atrial fibrillation) causes "**pain out of proportion to examination**", with a soft abdomen early and rising lactate. CT angiography confirms it. This is an emergency.

**Crohn's disease**: terminal ileitis causes right lower quadrant pain, diarrhoea and weight loss; it can mimic appendicitis. CT or MR enterography show "**skip lesions**", thickened bowel and the "**string sign**" from narrowing; complications include strictures, fistulae and abscesses.

**Meckel's diverticulum**: a remnant of the vitelline duct on the ileum. The "**rule of 2s**": about 2% of people, about 2 feet (60 cm) from the ileocaecal valve, about 2 inches long, often symptomatic before age 2. It may contain stomach lining and cause **painless bleeding** in children; a **technetium-99m pertechnetate scan** detects it.

**Terminal ileum resection** (over about 100 cm) causes **B12 deficiency** (with neurological complications), **bile acid diarrhoea** and fat malabsorption, and raises the risk of **gallstones** and **kidney stones**. Massive resection leads to **short bowel syndrome**.

**Intussusception** in toddlers (often starting at the ileocaecal region): episodic screaming, drawing up legs, "**redcurrant jelly**" stools, a sausage-shaped mass; ultrasound shows a "**target sign**".

keyPoints: Intraperitoneal on a mesentery; supplied by the SMA
Villi and microvilli give a huge absorptive surface
Terminal ileum absorbs B12 and bile acids
Peyer's patches are lymphoid tissue in the ileum
Commonest cause of adult small bowel obstruction: adhesions

test.explain: B12 bound to intrinsic factor is taken up by cubilin receptors in the terminal ileum.

test.q: Which feature is typical of the ileum rather than the jejunum?
test.explain: Peyer's patches are lymphoid clusters, most prominent in the ileum.

test.q: Which artery supplies the jejunum and ileum? (abbreviation or name)
test.explain: The SMA supplies the midgut, including the jejunum and ileum.

test.q: The lymph vessel inside each villus that absorbs fat is called a ______.
test.explain: Lacteals take up chylomicrons, which reach the blood through the thoracic duct.

test.q: A child has painless rectal bleeding; a scan shows stomach tissue in the ileum. Most likely?
test.explain: A Meckel's diverticulum can contain acid-secreting gastric tissue that ulcerates nearby ileum.
